aachen.s: Aachen is a city in western Germany that served as the favoured residence and principal court of Charlemagne. Its palace complex, including the Palatine Chapel, became the symbolic centre of the Carolingian Empire and the focus of its scholarly and administrative activity.

abbas-i-of-persia.s: Abbas I of Persia, known as Shah Abbas the Great, was the most celebrated ruler of the Safavid Empire, reigning from 1588 to 1629. He reorganised the army with slave soldiers (ghulams) and firearms, curbed the power of the Qizilbash, recovered territory from the Ottomans and…

abbas-ii-of-persia.s: Abbas II of Persia was a Safavid shah who ruled from 1642 to 1666. His reign was relatively stable and included the recovery of Kandahar from the Mughals, and he took a personal interest in government.

abbas-iii.s: Abbas III was an infant Safavid shah placed on the throne by the general Nader in 1732 as a nominal ruler. Real power lay entirely with Nader, who deposed him in 1736 and proclaimed himself shah at an assembly on the Mughan plain.

abbasid-caliphate.s: The Abbasid Caliphate was the Islamic caliphate that replaced the Umayyads in 750 and ruled from Baghdad, which it founded as its capital. Its early centuries were a golden age of trade, scholarship and science, but its political authority later fragmented among regional…

abbasid-revolution.s: The Abbasid Revolution was the uprising that overthrew the Umayyad Caliphate and brought the Abbasid dynasty to power in 750. Launched from Khurasan under the organiser Abu Muslim, it drew on discontent among non-Arab Muslims and supporters of the Prophet's family.

abbasid-shadow-caliphate.s: The Abbasid shadow caliphate was the line of Abbasid caliphs maintained in Cairo by the Mamluk Sultanate from 1261 to 1517, after the Mongol destruction of Baghdad. These caliphs held religious prestige and lent legitimacy to Mamluk sultans but had no real political power.

abd-al-karim-ibn-jama.s: Abd al-Karim ibn Jama was the founder of the Wadai Empire, traditionally dated to around c. 1611, when he led a successful revolt against the ruling Tunjur dynasty.

abd-al-malik-i-saadi-sultan.s: Abd al-Malik I was a sultan of the Saadi dynasty of Morocco in the 1570s. He led the Moroccan forces that defeated the Portuguese army of King Sebastian at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in 1578, although he died during the battle.

abd-al-malik-ibn-marwan.s: Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan was an Umayyad caliph who reigned from 685 to 705. He reunited the caliphate after a period of civil war, made Arabic the language of administration and introduced a distinctively Islamic gold and silver coinage.

abd-al-mumin.s: Abd al-Mu'min was the first caliph of the Almohad Caliphate, proclaimed caliph c. 1133 as successor to the movement's founder Ibn Tumart.

abd-al-rahman-i.s: Abd al-Rahman I was an Umayyad prince who escaped the massacre of his family during the Abbasid Revolution and fled to al-Andalus. In 756 he established an independent Umayyad emirate based at Córdoba, which never recognised Abbasid authority.

abdallah-al-mahdi-billah.s: Abdallah al-Mahdi Billah was the founder of the Fatimid Caliphate, proclaimed caliph in 909 in Ifriqiya. An Ismaili imam who claimed descent from Fatima, the Prophet's daughter, he came to power after the missionary campaign of Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i among the Kutama Berbers…

abdallah-ibn-yasin.s: Abdallah ibn Yasin was a Maliki religious scholar and preacher who founded the Almoravid movement among the Sanhaja Berbers of the western Sahara around the mid-eleventh century. He was brought to the desert after the Gudala chieftain Yahya ibn Ibrahim sought a teacher on the…

abdullahi-dan-fodio.s: Abdullahi dan Fodio was the younger brother of Usman dan Fodio and a leading scholar, poet and commander of the jihad that created the Sokoto Caliphate in the early nineteenth century. After the conquests, he was given authority over the western part of the caliphate, centred…

abeche.s: Abéché is a city in eastern Chad that became the capital of the Wadai Empire. It served as the sultanate's political and commercial centre, linked to trans-Saharan trade routes running northwards to Libya.

abeokuta.s: Abeokuta is a city in south-western Nigeria founded in the 1830s by Egba Yoruba refugees. Its foundation was one consequence of the wars and population movements that followed the collapse of the Oyo Empire.

abhijnanasakuntalam.s: Abhijnanasakuntalam, often called Shakuntala, is a Sanskrit drama by the poet Kalidasa. It tells the story of the love between King Dushyanta and Shakuntala, and it is regarded as one of the masterpieces of classical Indian literature.

abi-eshuh.s: Abi-Eshuh was a king of the First Dynasty of Babylon and a successor of Hammurabi's line. The Babylonian Empire's profile notes his failed campaign against the Sealand Dynasty in southern Mesopotamia.

abiodun.s: Abiodun was an Alaafin, or king, of the Oyo Empire who reigned c. 1770–1789.

abipa.s: Abipa was an Alaafin of Oyo who, around c. 1610, led the return of the Oyo court to its old capital Oyo-Ile after a long exile.

abolition-of-the-atlantic-slave-trade.n: Abolition of the Atlantic slave trade
abolition-of-the-atlantic-slave-trade.s: The abolition of the Atlantic slave trade refers to the outlawing of the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans, beginning with the British Slave Trade Act of 1807, which Britain then enforced at sea. The suppression of the trade disrupted economies on the West African coast…

abolition-of-the-ottoman-sultanate.s: The abolition of the Ottoman sultanate was the decision of the Grand National Assembly in Ankara in 1922 to end the office of sultan. The last sultan, Mehmed VI, left Istanbul shortly afterwards, and the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed in 1923.

abu-abdallah-al-shii.s: Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i was an Ismaili missionary who converted and organised the Kutama Berbers of what is now Algeria in the late ninth century. Leading them in war, he overthrew the Aghlabid dynasty of Ifriqiya.

abu-al-abbas-al-saffah.s: Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah was the first caliph of the Abbasid Caliphate, reigning from 750 to 754. He was proclaimed caliph during the Abbasid Revolution, and his forces defeated the last Umayyad caliph.

abu-al-fath-khan-zand.s: Abu al-Fath Khan Zand was a son of Karim Khan Zand, the founder of the Zand Empire. After his father's death in 1779 he was quickly deposed by Ali Murad Khan.

abu-bakr-al-siddiq.s: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq was a close companion of the Prophet Muhammad and the first caliph of the Rashidun Caliphate, ruling from 632 to 634. He suppressed the revolts known as the Ridda wars, reuniting Arabia under Muslim rule.

abu-bakr-ibn-muhammad.s: Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad was a sultan of the Walashma dynasty of the Adal Sultanate in the early sixteenth century. During the ascendancy of Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, he was kept on the throne as a nominal figurehead while real power lay with the imam.

abu-bakr-ibn-umar.s: Abu Bakr ibn Umar was an Almoravid leader of the Lamtuna Berbers in the eleventh century. After leaving northern operations to his cousin Yusuf ibn Tashfin, he returned to the Sahara and campaigned in the south.

abu-imran-al-fasi.s: Abu Imran al-Fasi was a Moroccan Maliki jurist who taught in Kairouan in the early eleventh century. Around 1040 he persuaded the Gudala chieftain Yahya ibn Ibrahim to bring a religious teacher to the Sahara, which led to the arrival of Abdallah ibn Yasin.

abu-muslim.s: Abu Muslim was the Persian revolutionary leader who organised the Abbasid movement in Khurasan and led the uprising against the Umayyad Caliphate. His armies were decisive in bringing the Abbasids to power in 750.

abu-said-bahadur-khan.s: Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan was the last effective ruler of the Ilkhanate, the Mongol state centred on Iran. His reign saw peace with the Mamluks but also rivalry among powerful amirs.

abu-yaqub-yusuf-i.s: Abu Yaqub Yusuf I was the second caliph of the Almohad Caliphate, son and successor of Abd al-Mu'min. He consolidated Almohad rule in the Maghreb and al-Andalus and was a patron of learning, supporting philosophers such as Ibn Tufayl and Ibn Rushd (Averroes).

academia-imperial-de-belas-artes.s: The Academia Imperial de Belas Artes was the Imperial Academy of Fine Arts in Rio de Janeiro, the main official art institution of the Brazilian Empire. It grew out of a group of French artists invited to Brazil in the early nineteenth century and trained generations of…

academy-of-gundishapur.s: The Academy of Gundishapur was a centre of learning in the city of Gundishapur in south-western Iran under the Sasanian Empire. It was especially noted for medicine and brought together Greek, Syriac, Persian and Indian knowledge.

acadia.s: Acadia was a French colony in north-eastern North America, covering parts of present-day Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and neighbouring areas. Founded in the early seventeenth century, it was one of the first French settlements in the Americas and part of the foundation of the…

acamapichtli.s: Acamapichtli was the first tlatoani, or ruler, of Tenochtitlan, reigning c. 1376–1395.

acapulco.s: Acapulco is a port on the Pacific coast of Mexico. Under the Spanish Empire it was the American terminus of the Manila galleons, which carried silver from New Spain to the Philippines and returned with Chinese silks, porcelain and other Asian goods.

achaemenid-empire.s: The Achaemenid Empire was the first Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in the sixth century BCE and stretching at its height from the Aegean to the Indus. It governed through satrapies, royal roads and a policy of tolerating local customs and religions.

acre.s: Acre is a port city on the coast of present-day northern Israel. In the era of the Crusades it was a major Crusader stronghold and trading centre, taken by Saladin in 1187 and recaptured during the Third Crusade, which made it central to the conflicts of the Ayyubid Empire.

act-of-abjuration.s: The Act of Abjuration was the declaration of 1581 by which the northern provinces of the Low Countries formally renounced the sovereignty of Philip II of Spain. It was effectively a declaration of independence during the Dutch Revolt.

acts-of-union-1707.s: The Acts of Union 1707 were the parliamentary acts that united the Kingdom of England and the Kingdom of Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain in 1707. They created a single parliament and a common market, opening English colonial trade to Scots.

adad-nirari-i.s: Adad-nirari I was a king of the Middle Assyrian period in the thirteenth century BCE. He campaigned against the kingdom of Mitanni (Hanigalbat) and reduced it to Assyrian vassal status.

adal-sultanate.s: The Adal Sultanate was a Muslim state in the Horn of Africa, centred on the region of Harar and Zeila, which flourished from the fifteenth to the sixteenth century. It controlled trade routes linking the Ethiopian interior to the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

adat.s: Adat refers to the body of customary law and traditional practice in the Malay world and the Indonesian archipelago. It governed matters such as land, inheritance and social relations, often alongside religious law.

addis-ababa.s: Addis Ababa is the capital of Ethiopia, founded in the late nineteenth century under Emperor Menelik II. It became the political and administrative centre of the modern Ethiopian Empire.

al-adid.s: Al-Adid was the last caliph of the Fatimid Caliphate, who died in 1171. During his reign real power passed to his viziers, culminating in Saladin, who held the vizierate in Egypt.

al-adil.s: Al-Adil was the brother of Saladin and sultan of the Ayyubid realm from 1200 to 1218. After Saladin's death in 1193, rival heirs fought for Egypt and Syria, and al-Adil's patient statesmanship allowed him to reunify most of the realm by 1200.

adil-shah.s: Adil Shah was a nephew of Nader Shah who seized power in the Afsharid Empire after Nader's assassination in 1747. His rule was brief and contested, and he fought a civil war with his brother Ibrahim Shah in 1747–1748.

adinkra.s: Adinkra are visual symbols of the Akan peoples of Ghana, each representing a concept, proverb or value. They were printed or stamped on cloth and used on other objects, notably for ceremonial occasions.

adolo.s: Adolo was an Oba, or king, of the Benin Empire in the nineteenth century. According to the empire's profile, he restricted which goods could leave Benin in order to protect the royal monopoly over key export commodities.

adulis.s: Adulis was an ancient port on the Red Sea coast of present-day Eritrea. It was the main maritime gateway of the Aksumite Empire, linking the Ethiopian highlands to trade with Egypt, Arabia, the Roman world and India.

aegean.s: The Aegean is the arm of the Mediterranean Sea between Greece and Anatolia, scattered with numerous islands. It was a crossroads of trade and conflict for many empires, from the Hittite Empire's western contacts to the Achaemenid Empire's wars with the Greek cities.

aerial-bombardment.s: Aerial bombardment is the use of aircraft to drop bombs or other munitions on military or civilian targets. Italy was among the first states to use it in war, in Libya in 1911, and the Italian Empire employed it extensively in the invasion of Ethiopia in 1935–1936, including…

afar.s: The Afar are a Cushitic-speaking people of the Horn of Africa, living mainly in the arid lowlands of present-day Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti. Many were pastoralists, and they controlled routes between the highlands and the coast.

al-afdal.s: Al-Afdal was the eldest son of Saladin, who inherited Damascus on his father's death in 1193. He fought his brother al-Aziz for control of Syria and Egypt, and the struggle allowed their uncle al-Adil to reunify most of the Ayyubid realm by 1200.

al-afdal-shahanshah.s: Al-Afdal Shahanshah was a powerful vizier of the Fatimid Caliphate in the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries. In the succession crisis of 1094 he bypassed the designated heir Nizar in favour of al-Musta'li.

afghanistan.s: Afghanistan is a mountainous region of Central and South Asia lying between Iran, Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent. Its passes made it a key corridor for armies and trade, and it was contested or crossed by many empires, from the Maurya Empire to the Khwarazmian and…

afghans.s: The Afghans, historically often meaning the Pashtun tribes, are the peoples of the region of present-day Afghanistan and adjoining areas. Afghan warriors and dynasties played major roles in South Asian and Iranian history, including in the Delhi Sultanate's Lodi period.

afin.s: The Afin was the royal palace of the Alaafin, the king of the Oyo Empire, at the capital Oyo-Ile. It was the seat from which the sacred king governed and the centre of court life and palace administration.

afonja.s: Afonja was the Are-Ona-Kakanfo, the leading military commander of the Oyo Empire, based at Ilorin. Around c.

afonso-de-albuquerque.s: Afonso de Albuquerque was a Portuguese commander and governor of Portuguese India who held office from 1509 to 1515. He captured Goa, Malacca and Hormuz, establishing a network of fortified bases to control maritime trade in the Indian Ocean.

afonso-i-of-kongo.s: Afonso I of Kongo, also known as Nzinga Mbemba, was king of the Kongo Empire from 1509 to 1543. A committed Catholic, he promoted Christianity, literacy and ties with Portugal, while trying to strengthen royal authority.

africa.s: Africa is the second-largest continent and the home of many of the empires covered by the site, from the Kushite and Aksumite empires to the Mali, Songhai, Oyo and Ashanti empires. Its trade in gold, ivory, salt and later enslaved people connected it to the Mediterranean,…

african-diaspora.s: The African diaspora refers to the communities of people of African descent living outside Africa, largely created by the Atlantic slave trade. Enslaved people from regions such as the Kongo and Oyo empires carried languages, religious practices and cultural traditions to the…

afrikaners.s: The Afrikaners are a South African people descended mainly from Dutch settlers, together with German and French Huguenot immigrants, who arrived after the Dutch East India Company founded the Cape settlement in 1652. They developed the Afrikaans language from Dutch.

afshar-tribe.s: The Afshar are a Turkic tribe, one of the Qizilbash groups that supported the Safavid dynasty in Iran. Nader, the founder of the Afsharid Empire, came from an Afshar clan in Khurasan.

afsharid-empire.s: The Afsharid Empire was the Iranian state founded by Nader Shah, who deposed the last Safavid ruler in 1736. Nader built a powerful army, defeated the Ottomans and Afghans, and sacked Delhi in 1739, but his rule was harsh and fiscally exhausting.

aga-khan.s: Aga Khan is the hereditary title of the imam of the Nizari Ismaili Muslims, a title first granted in the nineteenth century. The Nizari line traces its origins to the succession dispute of 1094 within the Fatimid Caliphate.

agaja.s: Agaja was a king of Dahomey in the early eighteenth century who expanded his kingdom towards the coast, conquering Allada and Whydah. His conquests disrupted the Atlantic slave trade network managed by coastal tributaries of the Oyo Empire.

age-of-discovery.s: The Age of Discovery refers to the period from the fifteenth to the seventeenth century when European navigators, led by Portugal and Spain, explored oceans and established sea routes to Africa, Asia and the Americas. It shifted global trade towards Atlantic and oceanic routes.

age-of-enlightenment.s: The Age of Enlightenment was an intellectual movement of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries that emphasised reason, science, individual rights and reform of government. It shaped political thought across Europe and beyond.

age-of-liberty.s: The Age of Liberty was the period in Swedish history from 1718 to 1772 when royal power was sharply limited and Parliament (the Riksdag) dominated government. It followed the death of Charles XII and the end of Sweden's great-power era.

agha-mohammad-khan-qajar.s: Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar was the founder of the Qajar dynasty of Iran in the late eighteenth century. He defeated the last Zand rulers and reunited Iran under Qajar rule.

agora.s: An agora was the central public space of an ancient Greek city, used for markets, assemblies and civic life. Greek-style cities with agoras, theatres and gymnasia were founded across Western Asia after the conquests of Alexander.

agra.s: Agra is a city on the Yamuna River in northern India. It was one of the main capitals of the Mughal Empire, home to the Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal, built by Shah Jahan.

agricultural-surplus.s: Agricultural surplus refers to the production of more food than farmers need for their own subsistence, which allows states to feed armies, cities, officials and religious institutions. Many empires rose on fertile river valleys or irrigated lands that generated such…

ahmad-al-mansur.s: Ahmad al-Mansur was the Saadi sultan of Morocco from 1578 to 1603, enriched by his victory over the Portuguese at Alcácer Quibir. Seeking control of West African gold and salt, he sent an army equipped with firearms across the Sahara, which defeated the Songhai Empire at the…

ahmad-baba-al-timbukti.s: Ahmad Baba al-Timbukti was a celebrated scholar and jurist of Timbuktu in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth century. He belonged to the city's learned elite, which provided judges and teachers under the Songhai Empire.

ahmad-ibn-ibrahim-al-ghazi.s: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, known as Ahmad Gragn, was the imam and military leader of the Adal Sultanate who led a jihad against the Ethiopian Empire from 1527 to 1543. Using firearms and Ottoman support, he conquered much of the Ethiopian highlands.

ahmad-sanjar.s: Ahmad Sanjar was a Seljuk sultan who ruled from Khurasan in the first half of the twelfth century, the last ruler to hold authority over much of the Great Seljuk realm. His defeat by the Qara Khitai at the Battle of Qatwan in 1141 and his later capture by Oghuz tribes weakened…

ahmad-shah-abdali.s: Ahmad Shah Abdali, also known as Ahmad Shah Durrani, was an Afghan commander in Nader Shah's army who founded the Durrani Empire after Nader's death in 1747. He invaded northern India several times and defeated the Marathas at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.

ahmed-bukr.s: Ahmed Bukr was a sultan of the Darfur Sultanate who reigned c. 1682–1722.

ahmed-sekou-toure.s: Ahmed Sékou Touré was a Guinean political leader and the first president of independent Guinea. In 1958 he led Guinea to reject the French Community in a referendum, making it the first French colony in sub-Saharan Africa to choose immediate independence.

ahmose-i.s: Ahmose I was the pharaoh who founded the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt around c. 1550 BCE.

ahuitzotl.s: Ahuitzotl was the eighth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, reigning from 1486 to 1502. He led extensive military campaigns that expanded the Aztec Empire to its greatest extent, reaching as far as the Pacific coast and areas near present-day Guatemala.

aircraft-carrier.s: An aircraft carrier is a warship designed to carry, launch and recover aircraft, serving as a mobile air base at sea. The Empire of Japan built one of the world's most capable carrier fleets in the interwar years and used it in the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941.

aisha.s: Aisha bint Abi Bakr was a wife of the Prophet Muhammad and daughter of the first caliph, Abu Bakr. She was an important transmitter of hadith and a respected religious authority.

ajele.s: The Ajele were royal representatives of the Alaafin of Oyo stationed in tributary towns of the Oyo Empire. They oversaw the collection of tribute and kept the provinces loyal to the capital.

akal-takht.s: The Akal Takht is the highest seat of temporal authority in Sikhism, located in the Golden Temple complex at Amritsar. It was established in the early seventeenth century by Guru Hargobind.

akan.s: The Akan are a group of peoples in present-day Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire who share related languages and cultural traditions, including matrilineal descent. The Asante, one of the Akan peoples, founded the Ashanti Empire in the late seventeenth century.

akbar.s: Akbar was the third Mughal emperor, reigning from 1556 to 1605. He expanded the empire across most of northern and central India and built an efficient administration based on the mansabdari system and a reformed land revenue.

akenzua-i.s: Akenzua I was an Oba of the Benin Empire in the early eighteenth century. After a period of civil conflict, he and his successor Eresoyen brought a partial recovery that stabilised the empire's core territories.

akhenaten.s: Akhenaten was an Egyptian pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty who reigned c. 1353–1336 BCE.

akhetaten.s: Akhetaten, known today as Amarna, was the capital city founded by the pharaoh Akhenaten in Middle Egypt in the fourteenth century BCE. It was abandoned soon after his death.

akitu.s: Akitu was the Mesopotamian New Year festival, celebrated most famously at Babylon in honour of the god Marduk. It included processions, religious rites and a ritual renewal of the king's authority.

akkad.s: Akkad was the capital city of the Akkadian Empire, founded or developed by Sargon in the twenty-fourth century BCE. Its exact location in Mesopotamia has never been identified.

akkadian-empire.s: The Akkadian Empire was the first known empire in Mesopotamia, founded by Sargon of Akkad around the twenty-fourth century BCE. It united the Sumerian city-states and extended its influence over neighbouring regions, including Elam.

akkadian-language.s: Akkadian is an extinct Semitic language of ancient Mesopotamia, written in cuneiform. It became the administrative language of the Akkadian Empire and later of the Babylonian and Assyrian states.

aksumite-conquest-of-kush.s: The Aksumite conquest of Kush was the campaign led by the Aksumite king Ezana around c. 350 CE against the Kingdom of Kush and its centre at Meroë.

aksumite-empire.s: The Aksumite Empire was a trading state centred on Aksum in the northern Ethiopian highlands and present-day Eritrea, flourishing from roughly the first to the seventh century CE. Through the port of Adulis it traded with Rome, Arabia and India, minted its own coins and…

aksumite-invasion-of-kush.s: The Aksumite invasion of Kush refers to military expeditions by the Aksumite Empire into the Kingdom of Kush in the c. 4th century CE, most notably under King Ezana.

akwamu.s: Akwamu was an Akan state in the forest and coastal region of present-day Ghana that was powerful in the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. It controlled trade routes to the coast and was a major regional rival.

ala-ad-din-muhammad-ii.s: Ala ad-Din Muhammad II was the shah of the Khwarazmian Empire from 1200 to 1220. He expanded his realm across Iran and Central Asia, making it one of the largest states in the Islamic world.

ala-ad-din-tekish.s: Ala ad-Din Tekish was the ruler of Khwarazm from 1172 to 1200. He freed the state from dependence on the Qara Khitai and defeated the last Seljuk sultan of Iraq, expanding into Iran.

alaafin.s: The Alaafin was the king of the Oyo Empire, a sacred ruler regarded as the embodiment of divine Yoruba kingship. He governed from the Afin palace at Oyo-Ile but was constrained by the Oyo Mesi, a council of seven hereditary chiefs who could demand his death.

alamut.s: Alamut is a mountain fortress in the Alborz range of northern Iran. From 1090 it was the headquarters of the Nizari Ismailis, sometimes called the Assassins, who resisted the Seljuk Empire.

alaric-i.s: Alaric I was a king of the Visigoths who led his people in conflicts with the Roman Empire in the late fourth and early fifth centuries. In 410 his forces sacked Rome, the first time the city had fallen to a foreign enemy in about eight centuries.

alaska.s: Alaska is a large region in north-western North America. It was colonised by the Russian Empire from the eighteenth century, mainly for the fur trade, and administered through the Russian-American Company.

alauddin-khalji.s: Alauddin Khalji was a sultan of the Delhi Sultanate who reigned from 1296 until his death in 1316. He repelled Mongol invasions, extended the sultanate's power into the Deccan and southern India, and introduced market price controls and stricter land revenue collection.

alban-berg.s: Alban Berg was an Austrian composer and a member of the Second Viennese School with Arnold Schoenberg and Anton Webern. He is known for works such as the opera Wozzeck.

albanians.s: The Albanians are a people of the western Balkans who speak the Albanian language. Under the Ottoman Empire many converted to Islam and served in the army and administration.

alborz.s: The Alborz is a mountain range in northern Iran, running along the southern side of the Caspian Sea. Its fortresses, including Alamut, became strongholds of the Nizari Ismailis after their split from the Fatimid Caliphate.

alcuin-of-york.s: Alcuin of York was an English scholar and teacher who joined the court of Charlemagne in the late eighth century. He led the palace school and played a leading role in the Carolingian Renaissance, promoting education, the copying of texts and reforms of script and liturgy.

aleppo.s: Aleppo is a major city in northern Syria with a long history as a trading and political centre. It was a key prize in the twelfth-century struggles of Nur al-Din and Saladin, whose control of it was central to the foundation of the Ayyubid Empire.

aleutian-islands.s: The Aleutian Islands are a chain of islands extending from Alaska towards Kamchatka in the North Pacific. In 1942, during the Second World War, the Empire of Japan occupied the islands of Attu and Kiska.

alexander-graham-bell.s: Alexander Graham Bell was a Scottish-born scientist and inventor credited with patenting the telephone in 1876. Emperor Pedro II of the Brazilian Empire met him at the Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia that year and was impressed by the device.

alexander-i-of-russia.s: Alexander I of Russia was emperor of the Russian Empire from 1801 to 1825. He led Russia through the Napoleonic Wars, including the defeat of Napoleon's invasion in 1812, and Russian armies reached Paris in 1814.

alexander-ii-of-russia.s: Alexander II of Russia was emperor of the Russian Empire from 1855 to 1881, known as the Tsar Liberator. His Great Reforms included the emancipation of the serfs in 1861, together with changes to local government, the courts and the army.

alexander-pushkin.s: Alexander Pushkin was a Russian poet, playwright and novelist of the early nineteenth century, widely regarded as the founder of modern Russian literature. His works include Eugene Onegin and Boris Godunov.

alexander-suvorov.s: Alexander Suvorov was a Russian general of the eighteenth century, famous for never losing a major battle. He won important victories against the Ottoman Empire, including the storming of Izmail in 1790, and commanded campaigns in Poland and Italy.

alexander-the-great.s: Alexander the Great, Alexander III of Macedon, was king of Macedon from 336 to 323 BCE. He conquered the Achaemenid Empire and led his army as far as the Indus valley, creating the Macedonian Empire.

alexanders-siege-of-gaza.s: Alexander's siege of Gaza was a siege by the army of Alexander the Great in 332 BCE, following the capture of Tyre, as he advanced towards Egypt. The city's Persian garrison resisted for some months before it was taken by storm.

alexanders-siege-of-tyre.s: Alexander's siege of Tyre was the siege of the Phoenician island city of Tyre by Alexander the Great in 332 BCE. To reach the city, his engineers built a causeway from the mainland, and Tyre fell after about seven months.

alexandria.s: Alexandria is a city on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BCE. Under the Ptolemaic Empire it became the capital, a major port and a centre of learning, home to the Library and the Pharos lighthouse.

alexei-brusilov.s: Alexei Brusilov was a Russian general in the First World War. His offensive of 1916 against Austro-Hungarian forces in Galicia and Volhynia inflicted very heavy losses.

alexios-i-komnenos.s: Alexios I Komnenos was Byzantine emperor from 1081 to 1118 and founder of the Komnenian dynasty. He restored the empire after defeats against the Seljuks and Normans, reformed its coinage and finances, and requested Western help that contributed to the First Crusade.

alfa-molo-balde.s: Alfa Molo Balde was a Fula leader of the nineteenth century who led a Muslim revolt against the Kaabu Empire. His forces, allied with the Fula of Futa Jallon, were involved in the overthrow of Kaabu, whose capital Kansala fell in 1867.

alfonso-i-of-aragon.s: Alfonso I of Aragon, known as the Battler, was king of Aragon and Navarre in the early twelfth century. He captured Zaragoza in 1118 and won other territories from Muslim rule in the Ebro valley.

alfonso-vi-of-castile.s: Alfonso VI of Castile was king of León and Castile in the late eleventh century. His capture of Toledo in 1085 alarmed the Muslim taifa kings, who invited the Almoravids from North Africa to help them.

alfonso-viii.s: Alfonso VIII was king of Castile from 1158 to 1214. After being defeated by the Almohads at Alarcos in 1195, he led a coalition of Christian kingdoms to a decisive victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.

alfred-von-tirpitz.s: Alfred von Tirpitz was a German admiral and State Secretary of the Imperial Naval Office from 1897 to 1916. He directed the build-up of the German High Seas Fleet under the naval laws, intended to challenge British naval supremacy.

algebra.s: Algebra is the branch of mathematics that deals with symbols and the rules for manipulating them to solve equations. Its name comes from the Arabic al-jabr in the title of a treatise by the ninth-century scholar al-Khwarizmi, who worked in Baghdad.

algeria.s: Algeria is a country in north-western Africa between the Mediterranean and the Sahara. Its territory formed part of medieval empires such as the Almoravid domains and was later an Ottoman province governed from Algiers.

algerian-war.s: The Algerian War was the war of independence fought by Algerian nationalists, led by the National Liberation Front, against French rule from 1954 until it ended in 1962. It involved guerrilla warfare, urban terrorism, counter-insurgency and widespread use of torture.

algiers.s: Algiers is the capital of Algeria and a major Mediterranean port. Under Ottoman rule it was the seat of a powerful regency.

ali-dinar.s: Ali Dinar was the last sultan of the Darfur Sultanate, who restored the sultanate in 1898 after the fall of the Mahdist state. He ruled with considerable independence under nominal recognition of Anglo-Egyptian authority.

ali-ibn-abi-talib.s: Ali ibn Abi Talib was the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad and the fourth caliph of the Rashidun Caliphate, ruling from 656 to 661 CE. His caliphate was marked by civil war, including conflict with Mu'awiya, who went on to found the Umayyad Caliphate after Ali's…

ali-ibn-yusuf.s: Ali ibn Yusuf was the Almoravid ruler from 1106 to 1143, son of Yusuf ibn Tashfin. He presided over the empire at its greatest extent, including al-Andalus, and supported building and religious scholarship.

ali-murad-khan-zand.s: Ali Murad Khan Zand was a ruler of the Zand dynasty of Iran in the years after the death of Karim Khan Zand in 1779. He deposed Karim Khan's son Abu al-Fath Khan and fought rival claimants for the throne.

ali-qapu.s: The Ali Qapu is a palace on the western side of Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan, built under the Safavid Empire around the reign of Abbas I. It served as a grand gateway and reception palace, with an elevated veranda from which the shah viewed events in the square.

ali-shir-navai.s: Ali-Shir Nava'i was a poet, statesman and patron of the arts at the Timurid court of Herat in the late fifteenth century. He wrote extensively in Chagatai Turkic and argued for its literary merit alongside Persian.

alkali.s: Alkali, from the Arabic al-qadi, was the title of an Islamic judge in the Hausa and Fulani lands of West Africa. In the Sokoto Caliphate, alkalis administered Islamic law in the emirates.

allada.s: Allada was a kingdom of the Aja peoples on the coast of present-day Benin, an early centre of the Atlantic slave trade. It was conquered by Dahomey under King Agaja in the 1720s.

allahabad-pillar-inscription.s: The Allahabad Pillar Inscription is a text inscribed on an earlier Ashokan pillar now at Allahabad (Prayagraj) in northern India. It contains a eulogy of the Gupta emperor Samudragupta composed by the court poet Harishena, listing his conquests and the rulers who submitted to…

allied-invasion-of-sicily.s: The Allied invasion of Sicily was the Second World War campaign in 1943 in which British, American and Canadian forces landed on and captured Sicily. The invasion contributed to the overthrow of Mussolini in July 1943.

allies.s: The Allies, or Allied Powers, were the coalition that fought the Central Powers in the First World War, including France, the British Empire, Russia, Italy and later the United States. Their victory in 1918 led to the dissolution of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

almohad-caliphate.s: The Almohad Caliphate was a Berber Muslim empire founded on the religious reform movement of Ibn Tumart and established as a state by Abd al-Mu'min in the twelfth century. It overthrew the Almoravid Empire and ruled the Maghreb and al-Andalus, promoting a strict doctrine of…

almohad-conquest-of-marrakesh.s: The Almohad conquest of Marrakesh was the capture of the Almoravid capital by the forces of Abd al-Mu'min in 1147. The city was stormed after a siege, and the last Almoravid ruler there was killed.

almoravid-capture-of-awdaghast.s: The Almoravid capture of Awdaghast was the seizure of the Saharan trading town of Awdaghast by the Almoravids in 1054. Awdaghast was an important commercial centre linked to the Ghana Empire's control of the trans-Saharan gold trade.

almoravid-empire.s: The Almoravid Empire was a Berber Muslim empire that arose from a religious reform movement among the Sanhaja of the western Sahara in the eleventh century. Under leaders such as Yusuf ibn Tashfin it conquered Morocco, founded Marrakesh, and intervened in al-Andalus after 1086.

alp-arslan.s: Alp Arslan was sultan of the Seljuk Empire from 1063 to 1072. He is best known for his victory over the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, which opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

alps.s: The Alps are the major mountain range of south-central Europe, separating Italy from France, Switzerland, Germany and Austria. Hannibal's crossing of the Alps with an army and elephants in 218 BCE is one of the most famous episodes of the Punic Empire's wars with Rome.

alsace-lorraine.s: Alsace-Lorraine was the territory annexed by the German Empire from France after the Franco-Prussian War in 1871. It was administered as an imperial territory and became a lasting source of French resentment.

altai-mountains.s: The Altai Mountains are a mountain range in Central Asia where Russia, China, Mongolia and Kazakhstan meet. The region was an important homeland and pastureland for nomadic peoples of the steppe.

amari-ngone-sobel-fall.s: Amari Ngone Sobel Fall was a ruler of Cayor, a Wolof state that had been a vassal of the Jolof Empire. Around 1549 his forces defeated the imperial army at the Battle of Danki.

amarna-archive.s: The Amarna archive is the collection of clay tablets found at Amarna, the site of Akhenaten's capital Akhetaten in Egypt. It consists mainly of diplomatic letters in Akkadian between the Egyptian court and other rulers, including the kings of Babylon.

amarna-letters.s: The Amarna letters are a set of clay tablets from the 14th century BCE, discovered at Amarna in Egypt, recording diplomatic correspondence between Egyptian pharaohs and other rulers. Written mostly in Akkadian, the international language of the time, they include letters from…

amazon.s: The Amazon is the vast rainforest and river basin of northern South America, most of which lies in Brazil. Under the Brazilian Empire it remained a sparsely settled frontier region, and the government sought to assert control over its territory and river trade.

amda-seyon-i.s: Amda Seyon I was emperor of Ethiopia who acceded in 1314. He conducted successful campaigns against the Muslim states to the east and south, greatly expanding the power and territory of the Solomonic dynasty.

amenhotep-iii.s: Amenhotep III was a pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt in the fourteenth century BCE. His long reign was a period of peace, wealth and monumental building, and he conducted extensive diplomacy with other great powers.

american-south.s: The American South refers to the southern states of the United States, where plantation agriculture relied on enslaved African labour before the Civil War. The antebellum South is often used as a point of comparison in discussions of large-scale slavery.

americas.s: The Americas are the continents of North and South America and the Caribbean. They were home to indigenous states such as the Aztec Empire before European conquest and colonisation from 1492, led by the Spanish Empire and followed by Portugal, Britain, France and the Netherlands.

amhara.s: Amhara is a highland region in north-central Ethiopia, the homeland of the Amhara people. It was the heartland of the Solomonic dynasty that restored the Ethiopian monarchy in 1270.

amida.s: Amida was a fortified city on the Tigris in upper Mesopotamia, now Diyarbakır in Turkey. It was a strategic frontier stronghold disputed between the Roman Empire and the Sasanian Empire.

amir.s: Amir, meaning commander or prince in Arabic, is a title used across the Islamic world for military commanders, governors and rulers. In the Rashidun Caliphate amirs led armies and provinces, while in later states such as the Almoravid Empire, the Ilkhanate and the Timurid…

amir-title.s: Amir is an Arabic title meaning commander or prince, used for military and political leaders in the Islamic world. Timur, the founder of the Timurid Empire, ruled with the title of amir rather than khan, because he was not a descendant of Genghis Khan.

amir-al-muslimin.s: Amir al-Muslimin, meaning Commander of the Muslims, was the title adopted by the Almoravid rulers, notably Yusuf ibn Tashfin. It deliberately differed from the caliphal title Commander of the Faithful, acknowledging the religious authority of the Abbasid caliph.

amorite-wall.s: The Amorite Wall was a defensive wall built by kings of the Third Dynasty of Ur in Mesopotamia to keep out Amorite groups migrating from the west. It was constructed in the late third millennium BCE across the land north of Sumer.

amorites.s: The Amorites were a Semitic-speaking people of ancient Syria and Mesopotamia, originally seen by Mesopotamian sources as nomadic outsiders. In the late third millennium BCE their migrations put pressure on the Akkadian and Neo-Sumerian empires.

amphora.s: An amphora is a two-handled ceramic jar used in the ancient Mediterranean world to transport and store goods such as wine and olive oil. Finds of Roman amphorae in the Fezzan of southern Libya show that the Garamantian Empire imported Mediterranean goods.

amr-ibn-al-as.s: Amr ibn al-As was an Arab commander and companion of the Prophet Muhammad. He led the conquest of Egypt for the Rashidun Caliphate in the 640s and served as its first Muslim governor, founding Fustat.

amritsar.s: Amritsar is a city in the Punjab region of north-western India and the spiritual centre of Sikhism, home to the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple. Under the Sikh Empire it was a major religious, commercial and political centre, and Ranjit Singh lavished patronage on its shrines.

amsterdam.s: Amsterdam is the capital of the Netherlands and was the commercial and financial heart of the Dutch Republic in the seventeenth century. It hosted the headquarters of the Dutch East India Company's largest chamber, the Amsterdam Exchange Bank and a major stock market.

amun.s: Amun was an ancient Egyptian god who, combined with the sun god as Amun-Ra, became the chief state deity of the New Kingdom. His temples at Karnak and Thebes received vast wealth from royal conquests, and the priesthood of Amun became a major economic and political force,…

an-lushan.s: An Lushan was a general of Sogdian and Turkic descent who commanded powerful frontier armies in north-eastern China under the Tang Dynasty. Favoured at the court of Emperor Xuanzong, he accumulated control of several military commands.

an-lushan-rebellion.s: The An Lushan Rebellion was a devastating revolt against the Tang Dynasty that lasted from 755 to 763. Launched by the general An Lushan and continued by his successors, it captured both capitals and caused enormous loss of life and disruption.

anabasis.s: The Anabasis is a work by the Greek writer Xenophon describing the expedition of the Ten Thousand, Greek mercenaries who fought for Cyrus the Younger against his brother Artaxerxes II around 401 BCE. After Cyrus's death the Greeks marched back through the Persian interior to…

anabasis-of-antiochus-iii.s: The Anabasis of Antiochus III was the great eastern campaign of the Seleucid king Antiochus III from 212 to 205 BCE. He marched through Armenia, Parthia and Bactria and reached the borders of India, reasserting Seleucid authority over rulers who had broken away.

anarchy-at-samarra.s: The Anarchy at Samarra was a period of turmoil in the Abbasid Caliphate from 861 to 870, when the caliphs ruled from Samarra. It began with the murder of the caliph al-Mutawakkil by Turkish military officers, after which several caliphs were made and unmade by the army.

anatolia.s: Anatolia, or Asia Minor, is the large peninsula forming most of present-day Turkey, between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. It was the heartland of the Hittite Empire and was later ruled or contested by the Achaemenid, Seleucid and Byzantine empires.

al-andalus.s: Al-Andalus was the name given to the parts of the Iberian Peninsula under Muslim rule from 711 until 1492. It was conquered under the Umayyad Caliphate and later ruled by an independent Umayyad dynasty at Córdoba, outside Abbasid control.

andalusia.s: Andalusia is a region of southern Spain, whose name derives from al-Andalus. Its cities, including Seville, Córdoba and Granada, were centres of Islamic culture and power.

angkor.s: Angkor was the capital region of the Khmer Empire in present-day Cambodia, flourishing from the ninth to the fifteenth century. It contained great temple complexes and an extensive network of reservoirs and canals that supported a large population.

angkor-thom.s: Angkor Thom was a walled royal city built by the Khmer king Jayavarman VII in the late twelfth century. At its centre stands the Bayon temple, famous for its many carved stone faces.

angkor-wat.s: Angkor Wat is a vast temple complex at Angkor in Cambodia, built in the twelfth century under King Suryavarman II and originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu. It later became a Buddhist site.

anglo-ashanti-wars.s: The Anglo-Ashanti Wars were a series of conflicts between the Ashanti Empire and the British between 1824 and 1901. The Ashanti won early victories, but British expeditions burned Kumasi in 1874 and exiled the Asantehene in 1896.

anglo-dutch-treaty-of-1824.s: The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 was an agreement between Britain and the Netherlands that divided their spheres of influence in maritime South-East Asia. Britain took control of the Malay Peninsula, including Malacca and Singapore, while the Netherlands kept the islands to the…

anglo-dutch-wars.s: The Anglo-Dutch Wars were a series of naval wars fought between England and the Dutch Republic in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. They arose from commercial and maritime rivalry over trade and shipping.

anglo-egyptian-condominium.s: The Anglo-Egyptian Condominium was the arrangement by which Sudan was jointly ruled by Britain and Egypt from 1899 until 1956, with Britain holding effective power. Darfur under Sultan Ali Dinar initially kept considerable autonomy.

anglo-maratha-wars.s: The Anglo-Maratha Wars were three wars fought between the British East India Company and the Maratha Confederacy between 1775 and 1818. The first ended inconclusively, but the second and third broke Maratha military power.

anglo-russian-convention.s: The Anglo-Russian Convention was an agreement of 1907 between Britain and the Russian Empire settling their rivalries in Central Asia. It divided Persia into spheres of influence and recognised British influence in Afghanistan and the neutrality of Tibet.

anglo-sikh-treaty-of-1806.s: The Anglo-Sikh Treaty of 1806 was an agreement between Ranjit Singh and the British East India Company. Under it the Sikh ruler agreed not to support the Maratha chief Jaswant Rao Holkar, who had fled into the Punjab, and the British undertook not to interfere in Sikh territory.

angola.s: Angola is a country in south-western Africa that was a Portuguese colony from the late sixteenth century until 1975. It was a major source of enslaved Africans for the Atlantic slave trade, especially to Brazil.

animism.s: Animism refers to religious beliefs that attribute spiritual presence to natural features, animals, places and ancestors. Such traditional religions were widely practised in West and Central Africa.

annexation-of-the-punjab.s: The annexation of the Punjab was the incorporation of the Sikh Empire's territory into British India by the East India Company in 1849. It followed British victory in the Second Anglo-Sikh War.

anshan.s: Anshan was an ancient city in the highlands of south-western Iran, at the site of Tal-e Malyan in Fars. It was one of the principal centres of Elam, whose kings styled themselves rulers of Anshan and Susa.

anthony-eden.s: Anthony Eden was a British politician who served as Foreign Secretary and then as Prime Minister from 1955 to 1957. In 1956 he ordered military intervention in Egypt with France and Israel after Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal.

anthony-sherley.s: Anthony Sherley was an English adventurer who travelled to the court of Abbas I of Persia in 1598 with his brother Robert. He served the shah as an envoy to European courts seeking alliance against the Ottomans.

antigonid-dynasty.s: The Antigonid dynasty was a Hellenistic dynasty descended from Alexander's general Antigonus I Monophthalmus. It ruled Macedonia from the third century BCE until the Roman conquest in 168 BCE.

antigonus-i-monophthalmus.s: Antigonus I Monophthalmus, the 'One-Eyed', was a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great who became one of the most powerful successors after Alexander's death. He sought to reunite the empire and expelled Seleucus from Babylon for a time.

antioch.s: Antioch was an ancient city on the Orontes River near the Mediterranean coast in present-day Turkey. Founded by Seleucus I, it became the capital of the Seleucid Empire and later one of the great cities of the Roman East.

antioch-on-the-orontes.s: Antioch-on-the-Orontes was a city founded around 300 BCE by Seleucus I Nicator, named after his father Antiochus. It became the main royal capital and administrative centre of the Seleucid Empire in Syria.

antiochus-iii-the-great.s: Antiochus III the Great was a Seleucid king who reigned from 222 to 187 BCE. He restored Seleucid power in the east through his anabasis and took Coele-Syria from the Ptolemies.

antiochus-iv-epiphanes.s: Antiochus IV Epiphanes was a Seleucid king who reigned from 175 to 164 BCE. He invaded Egypt but was forced by Rome to withdraw.

antiochus-vii-sidetes.s: Antiochus VII Sidetes was a Seleucid king who attempted to restore the dynasty's power in the second century BCE. He launched a major campaign to recover Mesopotamia and the east from the Parthians but was defeated and killed in 129 BCE.

anton-webern.s: Anton Webern was an Austrian composer and a member of the Second Viennese School with Arnold Schoenberg and Alban Berg. His concise, highly structured compositions influenced later twentieth-century music.

antonio-de-oliveira-salazar.s: António de Oliveira Salazar was the authoritarian leader of Portugal from 1932 to 1968, heading the Estado Novo regime. He insisted on keeping Portugal's African colonies, treating them as overseas provinces.

antwerp.s: Antwerp is a port city in present-day Belgium that was the leading commercial centre of northern Europe in the early sixteenth century. The Portuguese crown used it as the main European market for its Asian spices.

anushtegin-gharchai.s: Anushtegin Gharchai was a Turkic slave commander in the service of the Seljuks who was appointed governor of Khwarazm in the late eleventh century. His descendants held the governorship hereditarily.

anushteginid-dynasty.s: The Anushteginid dynasty was the ruling house of the Khwarazmian Empire, descended from Anushtegin Gharchai. Initially governors for the Seljuks, its rulers gradually won independence and, under Tekish and Ala ad-Din Muhammad II, built a large empire in Iran and Central Asia.

apil-sin.s: Apil-Sin was an early king of the First Dynasty of Babylon in the nineteenth century BCE and the grandfather of Hammurabi. He strengthened the city and built its walls.

appanage.s: An appanage is a grant of land or revenue given to junior members of a ruling family for their support. In the Mongol world, Genghis Khan divided his realm into appanages, or ulus, among his sons.

aq-qoyunlu.s: The Aq Qoyunlu, or 'White Sheep', were a Turkoman tribal confederation that ruled eastern Anatolia, Iraq and much of Iran in the second half of the fifteenth century. They expanded at the expense of Timurid territories in the west.

al-aqsa-mosque.s: The Al-Aqsa Mosque is a mosque on the Haram al-Sharif, or Temple Mount, in Jerusalem, one of the most important sites in Islam. Under Crusader rule it was converted to other uses.

aqueduct.s: An aqueduct is a channel or structure built to carry water from a source to a city, often across valleys on arches. The Romans built extensive aqueduct networks to supply baths, fountains and households throughout their territory.

aquifer.s: An aquifer is an underground layer of rock or sediment that holds water. The Garamantian Empire in the Sahara depended on fossil aquifers tapped by underground channels called foggaras to irrigate its oases, and their depletion is linked to its decline.

arab-conquest-of-the-fezzan.s: The Arab conquest of the Fezzan was the series of Muslim Arab campaigns into the Fezzan region of south-western Libya between 643 and 670 CE. Expeditions, including that associated with Uqba ibn Nafi, subdued the oases and imposed tribute.

arabia.s: Arabia is the region of the Arabian Peninsula in south-west Asia, bounded by the Red Sea, the Arabian Sea and the Persian Gulf. It was the birthplace of Islam and the starting point of the Rashidun Caliphate's conquests.

arabian-peninsula.s: The Arabian Peninsula is the large peninsula of south-west Asia between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. It was the base from which the Rashidun Caliphate launched the early Islamic conquests.

arabian-sea.s: The Arabian Sea is the part of the northern Indian Ocean between Arabia and the Indian subcontinent. It carried maritime trade linking the Persian Gulf, Red Sea and Indian ports.

arabic-language.s: Arabic is a Semitic language that spread with Islam from the Arabian Peninsula across the Middle East and North Africa. Under the Umayyad Caliphate it became the language of administration, replacing Greek and Persian in government records.

arabisation.s: Arabisation refers to the policy, begun under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik in the 690s, of making Arabic the official language of administration. Government registers previously kept in Greek or Persian were converted into Arabic, and a new Islamic coinage was introduced.

arab-khazar-wars.s: The Arab–Khazar wars were a series of conflicts in the seventh and eighth centuries between the Khazar Khaganate and the Umayyad and early Abbasid caliphates over control of the Caucasus. Both sides launched major invasions through the mountain passes.

arabs.s: The Arabs are a people originating in the Arabian Peninsula who speak Arabic. With the rise of Islam in the seventh century, Arab armies of the Rashidun and Umayyad caliphates conquered the Sasanian Empire and much of the Byzantine Empire.

arachosia.s: Arachosia was an ancient region in present-day southern Afghanistan, centred around Kandahar. It was an Achaemenid satrapy and was conquered by Alexander the Great.

aral-sea.s: The Aral Sea is a large inland lake in Central Asia, between present-day Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, fed by the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers. The steppe lands around it marked the northern fringes of the Achaemenid world.

aramaeans.s: The Aramaeans were a Semitic-speaking people of ancient Syria and Mesopotamia who formed numerous small states in the early first millennium BCE. Many settled in Babylonia, where they mixed with Chaldean and Babylonian populations.

aramaic.s: Aramaic is a Semitic language that became the common language of much of the Near East in the first millennium BCE. The Achaemenid Empire used it as an administrative language across its provinces, and it continued in use under the Seleucid Empire alongside Greek.

arcadius.s: Arcadius was Roman emperor in the East from 395 to 408, the elder son of Theodosius I. On his father's death the empire was divided between Arcadius in Constantinople and his brother Honorius in the West.

archery.s: Archery is the use of bows to shoot arrows in hunting and warfare. Mounted archers were the core of steppe armies such as those of the Mongol Empire, the Ilkhanate and the Khazar Khaganate, and of the Parthian Empire, famous for its horse archers.

ardabil.s: Ardabil is a city in north-western Iran. It was the home of the Safaviyya Sufi order founded by Sheikh Safi al-Din, whose shrine is located there.

ardashir-i.s: Ardashir I was the founder of the Sasanian Empire in Iran. Rising from Fars, he defeated the last Parthian king Artabanus IV in 224 CE and was crowned king of kings.

are-ona-kakanfo.s: The Are-Ona-Kakanfo was the title of the supreme field commander of the Oyo Empire's army. The holder was expected to be victorious in war and was traditionally stationed away from the capital.

arg-of-karim-khan.s: The Arg of Karim Khan is a citadel in Shiraz built in the 1760s under Karim Khan Zand, the founder of the Zand Empire. It served as his residence and fortified seat of government.

argentina.s: Argentina is a country in southern South America that emerged from the Spanish viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. In the nineteenth century it was a rival of the Brazilian Empire for influence in the Río de la Plata region, notably in the Cisplatine War, and later an ally in…

ariq-boke.s: Ariq Böke was a grandson of Genghis Khan and the youngest brother of Möngke and Kublai. After Möngke's death in 1259 he claimed the title of Great Khan with support in Mongolia, while Kublai claimed it in China.

aristotle.s: Aristotle was a Greek philosopher of the fourth century BCE whose works covered logic, ethics, politics and natural science. His writings were translated into Arabic under the Abbasid Caliphate and commented upon by Averroes under the Almohad Caliphate, and they were preserved…

armanum.s: Armanum was an ancient city in northern Mesopotamia or Syria whose exact location is uncertain. Akkadian royal inscriptions record that Naram-Sin conquered it together with Ebla.

armenia.s: Armenia is a highland region of the southern Caucasus and eastern Anatolia. For centuries it was a contested buffer between rival empires, including the Seleucids, Romans and Sasanians, and later the Ottomans and Iranian dynasties.

armenians.s: The Armenians are a people of the Armenian highlands with their own language and Christian church. Armenian merchants played major roles in long-distance trade, especially in the Safavid Empire, where Abbas I resettled them at New Julfa in Isfahan.

arminius.s: Arminius was a chieftain of the Germanic Cherusci who had served in the Roman army. In 9 CE he led an alliance of Germanic tribes that destroyed three Roman legions under Varus in the Teutoburg Forest.

armistice-of-11-november-1918.s: The Armistice of 11 November 1918 was the agreement that ended fighting on the Western Front between the Allies and Germany in the First World War. It was signed after Germany's military position collapsed and revolution broke out at home.

army-of-flanders.s: The Army of Flanders was the Spanish Habsburg army stationed in the Low Countries from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century. It fought the Dutch Revolt and other European wars and was one of the largest standing armies of its age.

arnold-schoenberg.s: Arnold Schoenberg was an Austrian composer who developed atonal music and later the twelve-tone method of composition. He led the Second Viennese School, whose members included Alban Berg and Anton Webern.

arquebus.s: The arquebus was an early form of matchlock firearm used from the fifteenth to the seventeenth century. Portuguese traders spread such weapons in Africa and Asia, and the Adal Sultanate employed matchlock-armed troops in its wars against Ethiopia.

arsaces-i.s: Arsaces I was the founder of the Arsacid dynasty and of the Parthian state, who seized the region of Parthia from Seleucid control around c. 247 BCE.

arsacid-dynasty.s: The Arsacid dynasty was the ruling family of the Parthian Empire, founded by Arsaces I in the third century BCE. It ruled Iran and Mesopotamia through a relatively decentralised system relying on powerful noble families and vassal kings.

art-nouveau.s: Art Nouveau was an international style of art, architecture and design that flourished around 1890–1910, known for flowing lines and natural forms. It drew strongly on Japanese woodblock prints and decorative arts, which became known in Europe after Japan's opening in the…

artabanus-iv.s: Artabanus IV was the last king of the Parthian Empire. He was defeated and killed in 224 CE by Ardashir I, who had risen from Fars.

artatama-i.s: Artatama I was a king of Mitanni in the fifteenth or fourteenth century BCE. He made peace with Egypt, and a daughter of his married the pharaoh Thutmose IV.

artaxerxes-iii.s: Artaxerxes III was an Achaemenid king who reigned from 358 BCE until he was assassinated in 338 BCE. He suppressed revolts and reconquered Egypt in 343 BCE, restoring royal authority.

arteshtaran.s: The arteshtaran were the warrior estate of Sasanian society in Iran, one of the main social classes alongside priests, scribes and commoners. It was made up largely of aristocratic families who provided the heavy cavalry.

arthashastra.s: The Arthashastra is an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, economics and military strategy, traditionally attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya), adviser to Chandragupta Maurya. It describes administration, taxation, espionage and diplomacy in detail.

aruna-pass.s: The Aruna pass is a narrow route through the Carmel ridge in present-day Israel leading to the plain of Megiddo. In the fifteenth century BCE Thutmose III led his army through this pass to surprise a coalition of Canaanite rulers at the Battle of Megiddo.

aryabhata.s: Aryabhata was an Indian mathematician and astronomer of the late 5th century CE. His work, the Aryabhatiya, dealt with arithmetic, algebra, trigonometry and astronomy, including an accurate approximation of pi and the idea that the earth rotates on its axis.

asantehene.s: The Asantehene is the title of the king of the Asante, the ruler of the Ashanti Empire. The office was established by Osei Tutu around the end of the seventeenth century and symbolised by the Golden Stool, the sacred throne of the nation.

ashanti-empire.s: The Ashanti Empire was an Akan state in present-day Ghana, founded by Osei Tutu around the end of the seventeenth century with its capital at Kumasi. Its power rested on gold, trade, including the Atlantic slave trade, and a strong army, and the Golden Stool symbolised its unity.

ashina-clan.s: The Ashina clan was the ruling family of the Göktürks, the Turkic people who founded the Gokturk Empire in the sixth century. Their leaders held the title of khagan and claimed divine legitimacy.

ashkenazi-jews.s: The Ashkenazi Jews are Jewish communities originating in medieval Central Europe. Many settled in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which offered relative tolerance and legal privileges, and it became home to the largest Jewish population in the world.

ashoka.s: Ashoka was a Maurya emperor who ruled most of the Indian subcontinent in the third century BCE and died in 232 BCE. After his bloody conquest of Kalinga he embraced Buddhism and promoted a policy of dhamma, publicised through inscriptions on rocks and pillars.

ashta-pradhan.s: The Ashta Pradhan was the council of eight ministers established by Shivaji, founder of the Maratha Empire. Each minister held responsibility for an area such as finance, foreign affairs, the army or religious matters, with the Peshwa as chief minister.

ashurbanipal.s: Ashurbanipal was king of the Assyrian Empire from 669 to 627 BCE, the last great Assyrian ruler. He campaigned in Egypt against the Kushite pharaohs, destroyed Susa and crushed Elam, and defeated a revolt by his brother in Babylon.

ashur-uballit-i.s: Ashur-uballit I was king of Assyria from 1365 to 1330 BCE. He freed Assyria from Mitanni domination and established it as a great power, corresponding with the Egyptian pharaoh as an equal.

ashur-uballit-ii.s: Ashur-uballit II was the last king of Assyria. After the fall of Nineveh to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BCE, he tried to continue resistance from Harran with Egyptian support.

asia.s: Asia is the largest continent, stretching from Anatolia and the Middle East to East Asia and the Pacific. It was home to many of the empires covered by the site, including the Achaemenid, Maurya, Han, Tang, Mongol, Mughal and Ming empires.

asia-minor.s: Asia Minor is the historical name for the Anatolian peninsula, the western part of Asia corresponding to most of present-day Turkey. After the Seljuk victory at Manzikert in 1071, Turkish groups conquered and settled much of it.

asiento.s: The asiento was a contract granted by the Spanish crown giving a person or company the right to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish America. In 1713 the Treaty of Utrecht granted the asiento to Britain, which passed it to the South Sea Company.

askia-ishaq-ii.s: Askia Ishaq II was the ruler of the Songhai Empire at the time of the Moroccan invasion. His army was defeated by Moroccan troops armed with firearms at the Battle of Tondibi in 1591.

askia-muhammad.s: Askia Muhammad, also known as Askia al-Hajj Muhammad or Muhammad Toure, was the ruler who seized power in the Songhai Empire in 1493 and founded the Askia dynasty. He expanded the empire, organised its administration and army, and promoted Islam and scholarship.

askia-muhammads-pilgrimage.s: Askia Muhammad's pilgrimage was the journey to Mecca made by the Songhai ruler Askia Muhammad between 1496 and 1498. During it he was recognised by the Abbasid shadow caliph in Cairo as his representative in West Africa.

asravan.s: The asravan were the priestly estate of Sasanian society, made up of the Zoroastrian clergy. They ranked at the top of the social hierarchy alongside the warriors and scribes.

assab-bay.s: Assab Bay is a bay on the Red Sea coast of present-day Eritrea. An Italian shipping company acquired land there in 1869, and the Italian state took it over in 1882.

assassination-of-archduke-franz-ferdinan.s: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, took place in Sarajevo in 1914. He and his wife were shot by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist.

assassination-of-julius-caesar.s: The assassination of Julius Caesar was the killing of the Roman dictator by a group of senators in Rome in 44 BCE. The conspirators aimed to restore the Republic, but his death led instead to further civil wars.

assassination-of-nader-shah.s: The assassination of Nader Shah was the killing of the founder of the Afsharid Empire by his own officers in 1747. His rule had become increasingly harsh, suspicious and fiscally oppressive.

assassination-of-rulers.s: The assassination of rulers is a recurring pattern in which kings, emperors or caliphs are murdered by rivals, courtiers, soldiers or conspirators. Such killings often triggered succession crises, civil wars or changes of dynasty.

assassination-of-uthman.s: The assassination of Uthman was the killing of the third Rashidun caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, by rebels in Medina in 656 CE. Discontent with his appointments and policies had led to unrest in the provinces.

assur.s: Assur was an ancient city on the Tigris in northern Iraq and the religious and original political capital of Assyria, named after its chief god. It remained the ceremonial centre of the Assyrian Empire even after the royal capital moved elsewhere.

assyrian-conquest-of-babylon-c-1225-bce.s: The Assyrian conquest of Babylon around c. 1225 BCE was the capture of the city by the Middle Assyrian king Tukulti-Ninurta I.

assyrian-conquest-of-egypt.s: The Assyrian conquest of Egypt was the invasion of Egypt by the Assyrian king Esarhaddon, who captured Memphis in 671 BCE and drove out the Kushite pharaoh Taharqa. Assyrian control was later reasserted by Ashurbanipal.

assyrian-destruction-of-susa.s: The Assyrian destruction of Susa was the sack of the Elamite capital by the army of Ashurbanipal in 646 BCE. The Assyrians looted the city, desecrated royal tombs and deported its population.

assyrian-empire.s: The Assyrian Empire was a Mesopotamian state centred on Assur and Nineveh on the upper Tigris. Rising as a great power in the fourteenth century BCE and reaching its height in the Neo-Assyrian period, it conquered Babylonia, the Levant, Elam and even Egypt using a highly…

astyages.s: Astyages was the last king of the Median Empire in the sixth century BCE. According to tradition he was the grandfather of Cyrus the Great, who revolted against him.

asyut.s: Asyut is a city on the Nile in Upper Egypt. It was the northern terminus of the Darb al-Arba'in, the 'Forty Days Road' caravan route that linked Darfur with Egypt.

atenism.s: Atenism was the religion promoted by the pharaoh Akhenaten in the fourteenth century BCE, centred on the worship of the Aten, the sun disc. It sidelined the traditional gods, especially Amun, and closed or neglected their temples.

athanasius-of-alexandria.s: Athanasius of Alexandria was patriarch of Alexandria in the fourth century and a leading defender of Nicene Christianity. He consecrated Frumentius as the first bishop of Aksum.

athens.s: Athens is a city in Greece that was a leading city-state of the classical era. It played a central role in resisting the Achaemenid Empire during the Persian Wars, including the victory at Marathon in 490 BCE.

atil.s: Atil was the capital of the Khazar Khaganate, located on the lower Volga near the Caspian Sea. It was a major trading centre, with communities of different religions, and the seat of the khagan and the government.

atlantic-ocean.s: The Atlantic Ocean separates Europe and Africa from the Americas. From the fifteenth century it became the main highway of European colonial expansion, used by the Portuguese, Spanish, British and French empires.

atlantic-slave-trade.s: The Atlantic slave trade was the forced transportation of millions of enslaved Africans to the Americas between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries. European traders, including the Portuguese and British, bought captives on the African coast from states such as the Kongo,…

atlas-mountains.s: The Atlas Mountains are a mountain range in north-western Africa, running through Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. The Almohad movement began among the Masmuda Berbers of the High Atlas, at Tinmel, from where it challenged the Almoravid Empire.

atomic-bombings-of-hiroshima-and-nagasak.n: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
atomic-bombings-of-hiroshima-and-nagasak.s: The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki were the attacks by the United States on two Japanese cities in August 1945, the only uses of nuclear weapons in war. They killed tens of thousands of people immediately and many more afterwards.

attack-on-pearl-harbor.s: The attack on Pearl Harbor was the surprise attack by the Empire of Japan's naval air forces on the United States Pacific Fleet in Hawaii on 7 December 1941. It aimed to cripple American naval power so Japan could seize resources in South-East Asia.

attic-standard.s: The Attic standard was the weight standard for silver coinage originating in Athens, based on a tetradrachm of about 17 grams. Alexander the Great adopted it for his coinage, and it became the common standard of the Hellenistic world.

attrition.s: Attrition refers to a form of warfare in which victory depends on wearing down the enemy's manpower and material resources through continuous losses. Such wars favour states with larger populations and industries.

audiencia.s: An audiencia was a high court of justice in the Spanish Empire, which in the Americas and the Philippines also exercised administrative and political functions. Its judges, called oidores, heard appeals and advised or checked the viceroys and governors.

augsburg.s: Augsburg is a city in Bavaria, southern Germany, and was a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire. In the sixteenth century it was home to the Fugger and Welser banking families, who financed emperors including Charles V.

auguste-comte.s: Auguste Comte was a French philosopher of the nineteenth century and the founder of positivism, which emphasised science, order and progress. His ideas were very influential among Brazilian army officers and engineers in the later Brazilian Empire.

augustus-roman-emperor.s: Augustus, born Gaius Octavius and known as Octavian before 27 BCE, was the first Roman emperor. He defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE and annexed Egypt, ending the Ptolemaic Empire.

augustus-ii-the-strong.s: Augustus II the Strong was Elector of Saxony and King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania, ruling for most of the period from 1697 to 1733. His involvement in the Great Northern War brought Swedish invasion and devastation to the Commonwealth, and he was temporarily deposed.

augustus-iii.s: Augustus III was Elector of Saxony and King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1733 to 1763. He owed his election to Russian and Austrian intervention in the War of the Polish Succession.

aurangzeb.s: Aurangzeb was the sixth Mughal emperor, reigning from 1658 to 1707. He expanded the Mughal Empire to its greatest territorial extent, especially in the Deccan, and enforced a more orthodox Islamic policy, including reimposing the jizya tax on non-Muslims.

australia.s: Australia is a continent and country in the southern hemisphere. Britain began colonising it in 1788 with a penal settlement at Sydney, and several self-governing colonies developed in the nineteenth century, uniting as the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901.

austria.s: Austria is a country in Central Europe with its capital at Vienna. It was the hereditary base of the Habsburg dynasty, which held the title of Holy Roman Emperor for most of the period from the fifteenth century.

austrian-empire.s: The Austrian Empire was the state ruled by the Habsburgs from 1804, when Francis II proclaimed himself Emperor of Austria, until 1867. It included Austria, Hungary, Bohemia, Galicia and parts of Italy.

austro-hungarian-compromise-of-1867.s: The Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867, or Ausgleich, was the agreement between the Habsburg monarchy and Hungary that created the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary. Hungary received its own parliament and government, while foreign affairs, the army and joint finances were…

austro-hungarian-empire.s: The Austro-Hungarian Empire, or Austria-Hungary, was a dual monarchy in Central Europe created by the Compromise of 1867 and ruled by the Habsburg emperor Franz Joseph and his successor. It combined many nationalities, whose tensions strained its political system.

austro-hungarian-ultimatum-to-serbia.s: The Austro-Hungarian ultimatum to Serbia was the list of demands issued by Austria-Hungary in July 1914 after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. It was designed to be difficult to accept in full.

austro-prussian-war.s: The Austro-Prussian War was a short war fought in 1866 between the Austrian Empire and Prussia, with their allies, for leadership in Germany. Prussia won decisively at the Battle of Königgrätz.

autocracy.s: Autocracy is a system of government in which supreme power is held by a single ruler, unconstrained by legal or institutional limits. The Russian tsars explicitly claimed autocratic power, and resistance to reform contributed to the Russian Empire's fall.

auxilia.s: The auxilia were the non-citizen troops of the Roman imperial army, recruited from provincial peoples. They provided infantry, cavalry and specialist units such as archers, serving alongside the citizen legions.

avar-campaign.s: The Avar campaign was a series of wars waged by Charlemagne and his commanders against the Avar Khaganate in the Pannonian basin between 791 and 803. The Franks captured the Avars' fortified 'Ring' and seized a great treasure.

avars.s: The Avars were a nomadic people who established a powerful khaganate in the Pannonian basin, roughly present-day Hungary, from the sixth century. They raided the Byzantine Empire and neighbouring lands.

averroes.s: Averroes, or Ibn Rushd, was an Andalusian philosopher, physician and judge of the twelfth century who served the Almohad caliphs. He wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle, which were later translated into Latin and shaped European scholasticism.

awash-river.s: The Awash River is a river in Ethiopia that flows from the central highlands towards the Afar lowlands. In the fourteenth century Emperor Amda Seyon launched expansion southward across the Awash, incorporating regions such as Dawaro and Bale and several Muslim sultanates.

awdaghast.s: Awdaghast was a trading town in the southern Sahara, in present-day Mauritania, that served as a terminus of trans-Saharan caravan routes. It was linked to the Ghana Empire and its gold trade.

awlad-al-balad.s: The awlad al-balad, meaning 'sons of the country', were the noble ruling elite of the Wadai Empire. They supplied the sultanate's standing cavalry.

awole.s: Awole was an Alaafin of the Oyo Empire in the late eighteenth century. His reign was marked by conflict with leading chiefs, including Afonja, the Are-Ona-Kakanfo at Ilorin.

axayacatl.s: Axayacatl was the sixth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, ruling in the later fifteenth century. He conquered the neighbouring city of Tlatelolco in 1473 and led campaigns in the Toluca valley.

axel-oxenstierna.s: Axel Oxenstierna was Lord High Chancellor of Sweden from 1612 until his death in 1654. He worked closely with Gustavus Adolphus to reform the central administration and led Swedish policy in the Thirty Years' War after the king's death.

axis-powers.s: The Axis powers were the alliance of Germany, Italy and Japan, with other partners, that fought the Allies in the Second World War. Fascist Italy joined Germany in 1940, but suffered heavy defeats in Africa and the Mediterranean.

aybak.s: Aybak, or Izz al-Din Aybak, was a Mamluk commander who became the first sultan of the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt in 1250. He married Shajar al-Durr, the widow of the last effective Ayyubid sultan, to legitimise his rule.

ayutthaya-kingdom.s: The Ayutthaya Kingdom was a Siamese state founded in 1351 in central Thailand. It expanded at the expense of the Khmer Empire and sacked Angkor in the fifteenth century.

ayyubid-empire.s: The Ayyubid Empire was a Sunni Muslim dynasty founded by Saladin, who ended the Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt in 1171 and united Egypt and Syria. Saladin's victory at Hattin in 1187 led to the recapture of Jerusalem from the Crusaders.

azad-khan-afghan.s: Azad Khan Afghan was an Afghan commander who rose to power in north-western Iran after the death of Nader Shah. He was one of the main rivals of Karim Khan Zand in the struggle for Iran.

azarmidokht.s: Azarmidokht was a Sasanian queen who ruled briefly around 630–631, during a period of rapid succession after the death of Khosrow II. She was one of two women, with her sister Boran, to occupy the Sasanian throne.

azcapotzalco.s: Azcapotzalco was the capital of the Tepanec state in the Valley of Mexico, which dominated the region in the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. The Mexica of Tenochtitlan were initially its tributaries.

azerbaijan.s: Azerbaijan is a region of the southern Caucasus and north-western Iran, centred historically on Tabriz. It was the heartland from which the Safavid dynasty rose and an important base of the Ilkhanate.

al-azhar.s: Al-Azhar is a mosque in Cairo begun in 970 under the Fatimid Caliphate, soon after the founding of the city. It became a centre of Ismaili teaching and later, under Sunni rulers, one of the most important centres of Islamic learning in the world.
